The underlying driving data comes from a population-wide simulation of the San Francisco Bay Area, and clusters of drivers were sampled proportionally to how common a given cluster was in the area. Therefore, the aggregation of our simulation results should generally resemble the optimal charging profile across all drivers based on the realistic mix of behaviors in the simulated region. This allows us to explore the potential grid- scale impacts of drivers charging in response to the price profiles modeled. Figure 36 shows the average daily shape of the total optimized charging profile in response to each price profile for each utility. On the Full tariff, each utility price profile results in a predominantly 8am-2pm charging shape. On the Medium and Mild tariffs, PG&E and SDG&E’s price profile (as driven by the modeled system net load profile) cause a slightly sharper daytime charging shape, while SCE’s price profile lends drivers to more early morning charging. This optimal charging shape impacts not only how EV loads show up on the grid in response to prices, but also how feasible it is for drivers to charge at the lowest-price hours. Under a Full dynamic tariff, with the modeled system net load profile, drivers would need to have access to daytime charging to fully realize the savings potential of the dynamic tariff. For many individuals, this would require workplace charging. If the system net load profile and dynamic price design result in a shape where the lowest prices in a given week often occur in the early mornings, individuals may benefit most by charging at home while they are sleeping. These results show optimal behaviors, but it is not known how more realistic (if suboptimal) behaviors impact the bill savings potential. Future work can model different scenarios of charging access and preferences to determine how it impacts charging behavior and costs. 52 Figure 36. Average daily charging shape for the entire simulated population of drivers in response to each price profile. Finally, Figure 37 shows the price customers pay for EV charging when they are able to fully optimize their charging behavior in response to dynamic prices. Values in this figure are converted to 2025 dollars, and a gasoline reference point of $4.75 is shown, using standard fuel economy, EV efficiency, and charging efficiency assumptions19. The top and bottom rows show the 2030 Low and High cost scenarios, respectively, while the individual panels show the results for each utility’s price profiles. In each panel, it is clear that customers pay the least amount for charging when they are exposed to the Full dynamic tariff, as the more dramatic price variations in this price profile offer hours with lower prices than the other profiles. On the Full tariff, there is also a wider range of prices (especially in the High price scenarios), showing that individuals’ driving patterns can cause more variation in those cases. On the Mild tariff, drivers all pay a more similar rate to charge, but that rate is always higher than on the Full or the Mild tariffs.
